text: Every password, no matter how strong, is a single piece of information: something the user knows. The trouble is that something you know can be stolen without the user doing anything wrong at all, through a phishing email, a data breach at some unrelated site where the same password got reused, or a keylogger on a compromised machine. Once an attacker has that one piece of information, a password-only system has nothing left standing in their way.

Multi-Factor Authentication closes that gap by requiring a second, independent proof of identity, something that category of attack doesn't also hand over. The two common real-world examples are a one-time code generated by an authenticator app, and a push notification sent to a trusted device the user has to approve. Both depend on physically possessing a specific device, a fundamentally different kind of proof than knowing a string of characters. MFA doesn't make passwords unstealable, phishing still works exactly as well as it ever did. What MFA changes is what that stolen password is worth afterward. Without the second factor, a stolen password alone is immediately sufficient to log in. With MFA in place, it accomplishes nothing on its own.

Here's the part that connects directly back to the SAML flow from the last lesson. Most organizations do not configure MFA natively inside ServiceNow itself. Instead, they enforce it at the Identity Provider, the same system that already sits at the enterprise's one authentication chokepoint. Mapped onto the seven-step SAML flow, MFA simply inserts itself into the step where the user authenticates at the IdP. The IdP now requires the password and the second factor before it issues the signed assertion ServiceNow is waiting for. ServiceNow's own role never changes; it still only ever receives and verifies a signed assertion.

That's a deliberate choice, not an oversight. Enforcing MFA at the IdP means it applies consistently across the entire application portfolio, ServiceNow included, rather than needing separate configuration application by application, the same scaling problem centralized password policy solved in the previous lesson. Because enforcement typically lives at the IdP, an MFA login failure is usually an IdP-side issue, a lost device, an expired code, an unapproved push notification, not a ServiceNow configuration problem. Confirming where the failure actually occurred is the first diagnostic step, the same classify-before-you-touch-anything discipline from the ACL work earlier in this course.

A password alone is something you know, and that alone is stealable. MFA adds something you have, and enterprises enforce it at the IdP so it covers every connected application at once. Next up, the Authentication Lab: a full worked scenario moving a real organization from local authentication to SSO with MFA enforced, walking through exactly how all three of these lessons come together in one real decision.
